title: Water, ice and citrus
lead: The two ingredients that never show on the menu: water and time.

sections.name: Water is an ingredient

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Melted ice is part of every drink.

know: An average cocktail ends up more than 25% water.
Too little water and it’s hot; too much and it’s thin.

video.title: 10 Chilling Factors to Cocktail Dilution | Course 2 - Lesson 09

keyPoints.line: of an average cocktail is water.

read.bigIdea: Every drink has water in it, and it’s on purpose.
read.where: When you shake or stir with ice, some of the ice **melts into the drink**. That water softens the alcohol and opens up the flavor. Dave Arnold’s class for Campari Academy puts an average cocktail at **more than 25% water**. Too little and the drink tastes **hot**; too much and it tastes **thin**.
read.mixup: Dilution isn’t watering a drink down. It’s part of the spec.
read.sayIt: It’s stirred on ice to open it up, so it’s smooth, not hot.

keyPoints.line: colder, lighter, cloudy: citrus, egg, cream.
goes into a shaken drink than a stirred one.

read.bigIdea: How you chill it changes the drink.
read.where: **Shaking** is hard and fast: it adds more **water** and **air**, so the drink comes out **colder, lighter and cloudy**. That suits drinks with **citrus, egg or cream**. **Stirring** is gentler: less water, no air, so the drink stays **clear and silky**. That suits **spirit-only** drinks like the Martini and Manhattan.
read.mixup: A shaken Martini isn’t wrong if a guest asks for it, but it will be cloudier and more watery than our spec.
read.sayIt: Would you like that shaken or stirred? Stirred keeps it clear and silky.

keyPoints.line: dry, hard ice. Wet ice adds water early.
melts slowly: for sipping over ice.
melts fast, for juleps and swizzles.

read.bigIdea: Ice is part of the build.
read.where: Use **fresh, dry ice**. Ice that’s been sitting wet in the well has already started melting and adds water you didn’t plan for. A **large cube** has less surface, so it melts **slowly**: right for an Old Fashioned. **Crushed ice** melts **fast**, which is the point in a julep.
read.mixup: Shaking with the big cube from the glass doesn’t chill or dilute the same way. Shake with fresh tin ice.
read.sayIt: It’s on one big cube, so it stays cold without watering down.

stops.name: Fresh, dry
stops.text: For shaking and stirring: no **early water**.

video.title: Juicing 101: The best way to keep juice fresh while at work

keyPoints.line: old lime juice won Dave Arnold’s blind test.
it’s worse. Juice for the shift.
it if it isn’t used soon.

read.where: In a 2010 blind tasting, Dave Arnold’s testers preferred **hand-pressed lime juice about four hours old** over juice squeezed that minute: it tasted rounder. The benefit doesn’t last: by the **next day** the juice has gone dull and bitter. So juice **at the start of the shift**, keep it **cold**, and don’t carry it over.
read.mixup: “Fresh” doesn’t mean squeezed this second. It means squeezed today.
read.sayIt: We juice our citrus fresh every day.

stops.name: Next day
stops.text: **Dull** and bitter: don’t carry it over.
